title: Plan to end chronic homelessness funding recommended
subtitle: Also: industrial land reserve deferred, community capacity fund, transit fares, police and conservation authority budgets.
overview: The Strategic Planning and Budget Committee recommended funding for the Plan to End Chronic Homelessness {{vote:m4}}, including an $11,124,967 increase to the 2024 Housing Services operating budget, paid from the Tax Stabilization Reserve and the property tax levy. It also recommended nine fee-for-service housing proposals totalling $3,113,493 {{vote:m3}}. A motion to defer both items and ask for a three-year phased plan was defeated {{vote:m5}}.

The committee deferred a proposed $5 million Industrial Land Readiness Reserve to its December 13 meeting {{vote:m7}}. It recommended a $1,000,000 annual Community Capacity Building Fund in the 2024 operating budget {{vote:m8}}. It rejected a proposal to hold the Grand River Transit cash fare at $3.75 and raise the monthly pass to $99 {{vote:m10}}.

Earlier, the committee heard 2024 budget presentations from the Grand River Conservation Authority and the Waterloo Regional Police Service, and received a Police Services Act memo for information. None of these were put to a motion. All decisions are recommendations to Regional Council. The committee meets next on November 29.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended implementing the interim plan, with an $11,124,967 increase to the 2024 Housing Services operating budget, a Homelessness Prevention Capital Reserve, a hybrid shelter capital amendment, and advocacy to other levels of government {{vote:m4}}.

The committee recommended funding nine housing service and program proposals for $3,113,493 from the 2024 tax levy, and asked staff to begin talks with Marillac Residence and YWCA Cambridge on possible new housing and a women's shelter {{vote:m3}}.
A motion to defer the homelessness plan and fee-for-service items and have staff return on December 13 with a three-year implementation plan was defeated {{vote:m5}}.
The committee deferred the proposed reserve, which included a $5 million 2024 contribution from the tax levy, to the December 13 committee meeting {{vote:m7}}.
As amended to $1,000,000, the committee recommended an annual fund in the 2024 operating budget, with staff to report in the first quarter of 2024 on terms of reference and timelines {{vote:m8}}.
A motion to keep the cash fare at $3.75 in 2024, raise the monthly pass to $99 from July 1 and increase the Affordable Transit Program discount to 52% was defeated {{vote:m10}}.

debate: On homelessness, staff said the crisis needs immediate tools and long-term housing work together, and that the gap would widen without action. One councillor questioned the cost of hybrid shelters against permanent housing and wanted a phased three-year plan because of tax affordability. Another said the people involved could not wait three years.

Councillors raised concerns about the size of the ask and the lack of measurable equity outcomes. Staff said an unallocated $2.4 million system stabilization fund would be shaped with community partners and brought back by spring. One councillor asked that the fee-for-service criteria be reviewed before next year, and another urged siting a future hybrid shelter and women's shelter in Cambridge.

On the police budget, one councillor questioned adding 18 officers when hiring has not filled existing vacancies, and asked for a report explaining salary surplus figures. The police board and chief said a consultant study recommended more front-line officers, that overtime is costly and unsustainable, and that hiring was phased over several years.

On industrial land, several councillors said a $5 million levy increase was too much in a tight tax year, while others said growth would add revenue later. Staff said debt financing is hard because the land would be sold, and the amount was flexible.

On the capacity fund, staff said the 2023 funding was one-time. The mover said the grassroots organizations it supported would lose funding, and the amount was reduced to $1,000,000. On transit, supporters of the cash fare freeze cited people paying with cash, and staff said fare capping would be considered in next year's business plan.
